content: Gram-positive bacteria are those that retain the crystal violet dye during the Gram staining process. Under a microscope, they appear blue or violet, in contrast to Gram-negative bacteria, which appear red or pink. The Gram classification system is based on differences in the structure of bacterial cell walls and is primarily used to visually differentiate bacterial groups for identification purposes. Gram-positive bacteria are characterized by a very thick cell wall composed of peptidoglycan. If a flagellum is present, it is supported by two rings, unlike the four rings found in Gram-negative bacteria, because Gram-positive bacteria have only a single membrane layer. Additionally, teichoic acids and lipoteichoic acids are present in their cell walls. These molecules act as chelating agents and play a role in bacterial adherence. Historically, Gram-positive bacteria were originally classified under the phylum Firmicutes, which remains the largest group. This group includes well-known genera such as Bacillus, Listeria, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Enterococcus, and Clostridium. The classification has since expanded to include Mollicutes, such as Mycoplasma, which lack cell walls and cannot be stained by the Gram method but are derived from Gram-positive forms. Another major group of Gram-positive bacteria is the Actinobacteria. Together, Firmicutes and Actinobacteria are referred to as the high and low G+C groups, based on the guanosine and cytosine content of their DNA. If the second membrane found in Gram-negative bacteria is a derived feature, Gram-positive bacteria may represent a basal form among bacteria. Alternatively, they could be a relatively recent monophyletic group. Gram-positive bacteria have been considered potential ancestors of archaea and eukaryotes due to their lack of a second membrane and certain biochemical similarities, such as the presence of sterols. The Deinococcus-Thermus group also exhibits Gram-positive staining, although structurally, they resemble Gram-negative bacteria. Both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria may possess a surface layer (S-layer). In Gram-negative bacteria, the S-layer is directly attached to the outer membrane, whereas in Gram-positive bacteria, it is attached to the peptidoglycan layer. A unique feature of Gram-positive bacteria is the presence of teichoic acids in their cell walls. Some teichoic acids, known as lipoteichoic acids, contain a lipid component that helps anchor the peptidoglycan layer to the membrane, as the lipid portion is embedded within the membrane.
